subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Dodo and Island Extinctions
description: A quick, practical guide to The Dodo and Island Extinctions.

hook.text: The dodo had no predators on Mauritius. It didn't know to fear the Dutch sailors who arrived in 1598.

buildup.text: Sailors hunted dodos for food. Rats, pigs, and monkeys they brought ate the eggs.

discovery.text: Within 80 years, every dodo was gone — one of the first documented human-caused extinctions.

twist.text: Islands are extinction traps — small populations, nowhere to flee, and sudden new predators.

climax.text: 90% of bird extinctions since 1500 have happened on islands, following the dodo pattern.

punchline.text: The dodo wasn't stupid. It just never needed to run — until it did.

quiz.question: Why are island species so vulnerable to extinction?
options: Small populations with no escape route

details.summary: The dodo, a flightless bird endemic to Mauritius, went extinct by 1681 after sailors and introduced animals destroyed its population. It symbolizes how island species with no evolutionary exposure to predators are devastatingly vulnerable to human arrival.
details.whyItMatters: Island extinctions account for the majority of recorded bird and reptile losses. The dodo's story illustrates why island conservation demands special urgency.
takeaways: The dodo had no predators and showed no fear of humans
Introduced rats, pigs, and monkeys destroyed eggs and habitat
Over 90 percent of bird extinctions since 1500 occurred on islands

faq.question: Why are island species so vulnerable to extinction?
faq.answer: Island species evolve in isolation with few predators, often losing flight, defensive behaviors, and large population sizes. When humans introduce rats, cats, or diseases, these naive species have no evolutionary defense and decline rapidly.

faq.question: How many island species have gone extinct since human contact?
faq.answer: Over 90 percent of all recorded bird extinctions since 1500 occurred on islands. Hawaii alone has lost more than 70 bird species. Island reptiles, snails, and plants show similarly devastating losses.
